probes.query: Application code receives a response but never closes it, and the call object is later reclaimed by the garbage collector. Explain what notices this and when that check runs, what it does to the connection that call was using, how the place where the call began can be captured and reported, and how the reporting differs on a server JVM, on an Android 11 or newer device, and on an older Android device. Name the file and component for each step.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Detection is in RealConnectionPool.pruneAndGetAllocationCount, called for every connection from closeConnections (the pool's cleanup task). Each connection keeps a list of RealCall.CallReference objects (weak references to the call); a reference whose get() is null means the call was garbage collected without finishing, so the pool reports it through Platform.get().logCloseableLeak(message, callReference.callStackTrace), removes the reference, and if no calls remain sets the connection's idleAtNs to now minus the keep-alive duration so it is evicted at once.

The creation site is captured in RealCall.callStart with Platform.get().getStackTraceForCloseable(...), stored in RealCall.callStackTrace, and copied into the CallReference by RealCall.acquireConnectionNoEvents when the call takes a connection.

CRITICAL: On a server JVM (base Platform) getStackTraceForCloseable returns a Throwable only if the OkHttpClient java.util.logging logger is loggable at FINE and otherwise null; logCloseableLeak then appends a hint to raise that logger to FINE when the trace is null and logs at WARN through Platform.log.

On Android 11+ (Android10Platform, SDK_INT >= 30) the captured object is an android.util.CloseGuard opened with the closer text and logCloseableLeak calls CloseGuard.warnIfOpen(); below SDK 30 (Android 10 itself and the older AndroidPlatform for API 21-28, which overrides neither function) the base Platform behaviour is used, and log is overridden to Log.w/Log.i with tag OkHttp.

On Android the FINE check depends on AndroidLog.enable(), called from PlatformRegistry.findPlatform: it maps the OkHttpClient logger to tag okhttp.OkHttpClient and sets its level to FINE only if Log.isLoggable(tag, DEBUG) at startup, so the stack trace exists on older Android only when that tag has debug logging enabled.

The check only runs when closeConnections runs: it is scheduled by scheduleCloser (on pool put and when a connection becomes idle), and closeConnections returns the keep-alive duration (default 5 minutes from the ConnectionPool defaults) while connections are in use, and -1 when the pool is empty; the Task.runOnce return value is the next delay and TaskRunner.afterRun reschedules unless it is -1.

probes.query: A server's cookie names a domain that is broader than the page host and is a registry-controlled suffix such as a country-code zone. Where does the client refuse it, which data does that decision consult, where does that data physically come from on a server JVM versus an Android app, and what must have happened in an Android app before the first such decision can succeed? Also say what a second thread sees while the first one is still loading the data, and what happens if loading fails. Name the file and component for each step.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Cookie parsing (Cookie.kt around lines 559-567) first requires the cookie domain to domain-match the URL host; if the domain is shorter than the host (not host-only) and PublicSuffixDatabase.get().getEffectiveTldPlusOne(domain) is null (the domain is itself a public suffix), the Set-Cookie is rejected (parse returns null).

PublicSuffixDatabase.getEffectiveTldPlusOne calls findMatchingRule, which first calls publicSuffixList.ensureLoaded(); the singleton instance is created as PublicSuffixDatabase(PublicSuffixList.Default), where Default is an expect val with one actual per source set.

CRITICAL: On a server JVM the actual Default (jvmMain PublicSuffixList.jvm.kt) is ResourcePublicSuffixList, reading the classpath resource okhttp3/internal/publicsuffix/PublicSuffixDatabase.list through FileSystem.RESOURCES; on Android the actual (androidMain PublicSuffixList.android.kt) is AssetPublicSuffixList, reading the asset PublicSuffixDatabase.list through PlatformRegistry.applicationContext?.assets (the file exists as androidMain/assets/PublicSuffixDatabase.list and jvmMain/resources/okhttp3/internal/publicsuffix/PublicSuffixDatabase.list).

On Android the application context is held by the platform object (AndroidPlatform or Android10Platform, both ContextAwarePlatform) through PlatformRegistry.applicationContext; it is set by the AndroidX Startup initializer PlatformInitializer (registered as meta-data in androidMain/AndroidManifest.xml) or by OkHttp.initialize(context), which only assigns when still null and uses the application context; without it AssetPublicSuffixList throws an IOException (message differs when Build.FINGERPRINT is null, a unit test without Robolectric).

BasePublicSuffixList.ensureLoaded lets the first caller win an AtomicBoolean compareAndSet and read the file (two length-prefixed byte blocks: the rule list and the exception list); other threads block on a CountDownLatch until the read completes.

If reading fails with an IOException, BasePublicSuffixList stores it as readFailure and ensureLoaded then throws IllegalStateException('Unable to load <path> resource.') with that cause, so cookie parsing fails with that exception rather than silently accepting.

probes.query: A server speaking the multiplexed protocol tells the client it is going away and names the last stream it processed. Trace what happens to the requests already in flight on that connection, what exception the application thread ends up with and where it is produced, how the connection's failure counters change, and how later calls are kept off that connection. Also say what happens to a call that tries to open a new stream just after the notice. Name the file and component for each step.
expectedFacts: Http2Reader.readGoAway validates the frame (length at least 8, stream id 0, a known error code) and hands lastStreamId, error code and debug data to the handler's goAway.

CRITICAL: Http2Connection.ReaderRunnable.goAway sets isShutdown = true and, for every stream with id greater than lastGoodStreamId that was initiated locally, calls Http2Stream.receiveRstStream(REFUSED_STREAM) and removeStream; streams with ids up to the named last stream are left running.

Http2Stream.receiveRstStream stores the error code and wakes waiters, so Http2Stream.takeHeaders (called by Http2ExchangeCodec.readResponseHeaders) or the body source read throws a StreamResetException carrying REFUSED_STREAM; Exchange.readResponseHeaders catches the IOException, calls trackFailure and rethrows.

Exchange.trackFailure calls codec.carrier.trackFailure, which is RealConnection.trackFailure: a StreamResetException with REFUSED_STREAM only increments refusedStreamCount, and only from the second one does it set noNewExchanges and increment routeFailureCount.

CRITICAL: Later calls are kept off the connection by health, not by those counters: Http2Connection.isHealthy returns false once isShutdown, so RealConnectionPool.callAcquirePooledConnection (after acquiring an eligible connection) and RealRoutePlanner.planReuseCallConnection mark it noNewExchanges, release it and close the socket if it is idle.

A call that races and opens a stream after the notice gets ConnectionShutdownException from Http2Connection.newStream (isShutdown); RealConnection.trackFailure treats it as noNewExchanges plus, if the connection has no successful call yet, connectFailed for the route and routeFailureCount++, and RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor.recover treats it as 'request not sent' (requestSendStarted false).

probes.query: A server tries to push an unrequested resource to the client over the multiplexed protocol. Trace what the client does from the moment the promise arrives: who is asked, what the default answer is and what the client sends back, and what happens to frames that later arrive for the promised stream. Also name the places that look as if they handle server-initiated streams or the client's push preference but do not apply to this case.
expectedFacts: Http2Reader.readPushPromise rejects stream id 0, reads the promised stream id and decodes the header block, then calls handler.pushPromise, which Http2Connection.ReaderRunnable.pushPromise forwards to pushRequestLater(promisedStreamId, headers).

CRITICAL: pushRequestLater answers PROTOCOL_ERROR (writeSynResetLater) if the promised id is already in currentPushRequests; otherwise it records the id and runs pushObserver.onRequest on the pushQueue task queue, and when that returns true (cancel) it writes RST_STREAM with ErrorCode.CANCEL and forgets the id.

CRITICAL: The observer on a client connection is the Http2Connection.Builder default PushObserver.CANCEL (nothing in RealConnection.startHttp2 or elsewhere in production code sets another): onRequest and onHeaders return true, onData skips the bytes and returns true, onReset does nothing.

Frames for pushed (even-numbered, nonzero) stream ids never reach the normal stream map: ReaderRunnable.data, headers and rstStream check pushedStream(streamId) first and call pushDataLater (reads the frame eagerly), pushHeadersLater and pushResetLater, each delegating to the observer and cancelling again.

Decoy: RealConnection.onStream (closes remotely initiated streams with REFUSED_STREAM) is the Http2Connection.Listener hook for peer-created streams, but the reader's pushedStream check routes even ids before listener.onStream is reachable for a client.

Decoy: Settings.getEnablePush is marked TODO (not honoured) and unused; the client's own SETTINGS (okHttpSettings) only set the 16 MiB initial window size and do not disable push; Http2Reader.readSettings only validates that a received ENABLE_PUSH value is 0 or 1.

probes.query: List every place along an ordinary request path where a time limit is armed, applied, or reset (leave out web sockets and the periodic liveness probe), and say which configured value feeds each one. Include how a fresh connection differs from a reused one, and how the two protocol versions differ.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The whole-call limit is RealCall.timeout, an AsyncTimeout set to client.callTimeoutMillis; it is entered in RealCall.execute and in AsyncCall.run, its timedOut cancels the call, and timeoutExit turns a fired timeout into InterruptedIOException('timeout'); upgrades and duplex calls stop it early through timeoutEarlyExit.

RealInterceptorChain holds the per-call connect, read and write values (initialised from the client, replaced through withConnectTimeout, withReadTimeout and withWriteTimeout, only before an exchange exists); RealCall.enterNetworkInterceptorExchange feeds them into RealRoutePlanner: connect becomes socketConnectTimeoutMillis, read becomes both readTimeoutMillis and socketReadTimeoutMillis, write becomes writeTimeoutMillis.

CRITICAL: For a fresh connection, ConnectPlan.connectSocket sets rawSocket.soTimeout to socketReadTimeoutMillis and calls Platform.connectSocket with socketConnectTimeoutMillis, so the read value also bounds reads during the TLS handshake; ConnectPlan.createTunnel sets the proxy CONNECT source and sink timeouts from readTimeoutMillis and writeTimeoutMillis.

RealConnection.newCodec runs for every exchange: for HTTP/1 it sets the socket soTimeout and the buffered source and sink timeouts to the current call's read and write values (so a reused connection adopts the new call's limits), and Http1ExchangeCodec.detachTimeout clears the per-exchange ForwardingTimeout when request or response bodies finish so limits are not shared between pooled uses.

For HTTP/2, RealConnection.startHttp2 sets the socket soTimeout to 0 because limits are per stream; Http2ExchangeCodec.writeRequestHeaders sets the stream's read and write timeouts from the chain values.
Http2Stream.doReadTimeout means a client stream enforces its read timeout only once the request body sink is closed or finished (matters for duplex calls).
probes.author: r3x-okhttp-drafter
probes.notes:

probes.query: On Android, the client may meet several different kinds of TLS socket: the one built into the operating system, one from a security-provider update delivered by Google's services, two from optional third-party security libraries, and one that exists only on the very newest OS release. For each kind, which component recognises it, what makes that component usable at all, and how does it switch on application-protocol negotiation? Also say which components are consulted on OS releases before Android 10, and which one is the only kind that can extract the trust manager from a custom socket factory.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: AndroidPlatform (API 21-28) builds its adapter list as StandardAndroidSocketAdapter.buildIfSupported(), DeferredSocketAdapter(AndroidSocketAdapter.playProviderFactory), DeferredSocketAdapter(ConscryptSocketAdapter.factory), DeferredSocketAdapter(BouncyCastleSocketAdapter.factory), filtered by isSupported(); Android10Platform (API 29+) instead starts with Android17SocketAdapter.buildIfSupported() and Android10SocketAdapter.buildIfSupported() followed by the same three deferred adapters; configureTlsExtensions and getSelectedProtocol use the first adapter whose matchesSocket is true, and with none (a custom socket class) no extension is configured.

The OS-built-in socket before Android 10 is recognised by StandardAndroidSocketAdapter (reflection on com.android.org.conscrypt OpenSSLSocketImpl, OpenSSLSocketFactoryImpl and SSLParametersImpl; it logs 'unable to load android socket classes' and yields null if the classes are missing) and configured by reflection in AndroidSocketAdapter (setUseSessionTickets, setAlpnProtocols with length-prefixed bytes, setHostname only on SDK 23 and below, getAlpnSelectedProtocol).

CRITICAL: The Google-services provider socket is matched purely by class-name prefix com.google.android.gms.org.conscrypt. through AndroidSocketAdapter.playProviderFactory (a DeferredSocketAdapter factory), then handled by the same reflective AndroidSocketAdapter, found by walking superclasses to OpenSSLSocketImpl; DeferredSocketAdapter creates its delegate lazily on the first matching socket and always reports isSupported true.

Android10SocketAdapter (usable when SDK_INT >= 29) matches sockets with SSLSockets.isSupportedSocket and configures session tickets plus SSLParameters.applicationProtocols using Platform.alpnProtocolNames; Android17SocketAdapter (usable when SDK_INT >= 37) does the same and additionally applies a parsed ECH config list, skipping an unparsable one.

ConscryptSocketAdapter is usable only if org.conscrypt classes load and Conscrypt.isAvailable() with version at least 2.1.0, matches with Conscrypt.isConscrypt(sslSocket), and sets session tickets and application protocols through Conscrypt; BouncyCastleSocketAdapter is usable only if org.bouncycastle.jsse.provider.BouncyCastleJsseProvider loads, matches sockets that are BCSSLSocket, and sets SSLParameters.applicationProtocols.

Only StandardAndroidSocketAdapter overrides matchesSocketFactory and trustManager (reflecting the sslParameters field and its x509TrustManager or trustManager field); the other adapters inherit the interface defaults (false and null), so AndroidPlatform.trustManager/Android10Platform.trustManager return null for any other factory.

probes.query: The DNS-over-HTTPS resolver keeps its own cache of answers, separate from the application's HTTP response cache. How long is an answer served, when does it get refreshed, how are failures and empty answers cached, and which record types share entries? Also say what bounds the number of entries and what decides which ones are evicted, and whether the operating system's default resolver goes through this cache. Name the file and component for each rule.
expectedFacts: The public DnsCache defaults are minimum TTL 10 s, maximum TTL 300 s, failure TTL 10 s, revalidate-before-expire 2 s and 1000 entries; it wraps a RealDnsCache and is used only by DnsOverHttps (Builder default DnsCache(); queryFactory = cache.-delegate.wrap(DnsOverHttpsQuery.Factory)); the default system resolver (Dns.SYSTEM, InetAddressDns) never goes through it.

CRITICAL: Entries are keyed by the DNS Question (name, type, class), so A, AAAA and HTTPS (service metadata) answers are cached separately; DnsOverHttps.newCall builds StateMachineDnsCall, which asks HTTPS (when includeServiceMetadata, with the _port._https. name for a non-443 port), AAAA (when includeIPv6) and A, while DnsOverHttps.lookup runs a copy with includeServiceMetadata = false that shares the same cache.

CRITICAL: RealDnsCache.CacheQuery.onResponse sets the lifetime to the minimum answer TTL (seconds) coerced into [minimumTimeToLive, maximumTimeToLive], or to failureTimeToLive when the response has no answers; revalidateAt = sentAt + max(0, lifetime - revalidateBeforeExpire) and expireAt = sentAt + lifetime. onFailure stores a Failure result for failureTimeToLive and replays that exception to queries until it expires.

CacheQuery.enqueue serves the stored result while now < expireAt, and starts a new network query when there is no result or now >= revalidateAt (so within the last revalidate window a still-valid answer is returned immediately while a refresh runs in the background); if the result is expired and a query is already in flight, the caller joins that in-flight call; cancelling a CacheQuery does not cancel the network query, so the cache is still updated.

MemoryCache.computeIfAbsent never evicts until the entry count reaches twice maxSize and then evicts down to maxSize in one batch (maxSize 0 disables caching: a new Entry each time and nothing stored); RealDnsCache.lastRequestedAt returns null for entries that are expired with no in-flight call (evicted unconditionally) and otherwise the last request time, and MemoryCache.evict removes the least recently requested using a priority queue that drops the newest.

probes.query: A client uses the default trust settings and has no certificate-fingerprint pins for the host it connects to. Does the library rebuild or tidy the presented certificate chain while it sets up the connection? Say where and when that tidying actually runs, how the component that does it is chosen on a server JVM versus on Android, what the tidied chain looks like, and what happens if the tidying fails. Name the file and component for each rule.
expectedFacts: OkHttpClient's init block, when the builder has no custom socket factory, takes Platform.get().platformTrustManager(), builds certificateChainCleaner = CertificateChainCleaner.get(trustManager) (which calls Platform.buildCertificateChainCleaner) and gives it to the pinner with withCertificateChainCleaner; with a custom factory the cleaner is computed in the Builder (from the supplied trust manager, or through Platform.trustManager for the legacy overload).

CRITICAL: The cleaner is chosen by Platform.buildCertificateChainCleaner: the base implementation is BasicCertificateChainCleaner over a BasicTrustRootIndex of the trust manager's accepted issuers; AndroidPlatform and Android10Platform override it to AndroidCertificateChainCleaner.buildIfSupported(trustManager) (which needs X509TrustManagerExtensions, i.e. a trust manager with the host-aware checkServerTrusted) and fall back to the base one when null.

CRITICAL: ConnectPlan.connectTls does not clean the chain eagerly: after the hostname verifier passes it builds the Handshake with a lambda that calls certificatePinner.certificateChainCleaner.clean(peerCertificates, host), then calls certificatePinner.check(host) { handshake.peerCertificates }; CertificatePinner.check calls findMatchingPins first and returns immediately when no pin matches the host, so the lambda never runs.
Handshake.peerCertificates is a lazy property over that provider: the cleaning runs on the first read, and a SSLPeerUnverifiedException thrown by it is swallowed, giving an empty list.

Readers that force it include RealConnection.isEligible for coalescing onto a different host (supportsUrl reads handshake.peerCertificates for the hostname check and the pinner check receives handshake().peerCertificates as an argument) and application code that reads Response.handshake().peerCertificates.

BasicCertificateChainCleaner.clean starts from the leaf, follows issuers (at most MAX_SIGNERS = 9) from the presented chain, appends the trusted anchor found via the TrustRootIndex unless it is already last, and throws SSLPeerUnverifiedException when no trusted certificate signed the chain or it is too long; the Android cleaner returns X509TrustManagerExtensions.checkServerTrusted(chain, 'RSA', host) and converts CertificateException into SSLPeerUnverifiedException.
